list.listitem: Assess support at every well child visit. In infants, assess parental support. In older children, assess support from family and friends. C
Assess development at every well child visit, including motor, social, school readiness, school performance and physical activity. C

Discuss behavior and discipline. Assess coping skills of and depression in parents and older children. Discuss the child's temperament, temper tantrums, parenting programs, proper discipline dependent on the child's developmental stage. C
Perform a complete exam, including measuring and plotting all growth parameters at every visit. C
Tailor anticipatory guidance to the child's developmental stage and parental concerns. C
Provide age-appropriate immunization and screening. A

Well child care visits are regularly scheduled visits designed to address parents' and patient's concerns, provide health supervision, monitor growth/development, provide anticipatory guidance, and provide immunizations.

The leading causes of death in children between 1 and 19 years are accidents and assault. Well child visits decrease accidents, injuries, and avoidable hospitalizations and improve immunization rates. One study found that children who are up to date on their Well Child visits were 48% less likely to "experience an avoidable hospitalization." Another study found that by 24 months of age, 87% of children with an adequate number of well child visits are up to date on their immunizations, as compared to 67% of children with an inadequate number of well child visits.
Refer to for specific well child care recommendations by age of child.
Elicit and address parents' and patient's questions and concerns. Obtain an interim history, namely that which has occurred since the last well child visit.
Discuss support systems in place and relationships. For younger children, discuss parental support systems. For older children, discuss friendships, peer pressure, and relationships.
Measure and plot growth parameters (including Body Mass Index in children older than 2 years of age). See chapter on obesity and weight loss.
Observe parent-child and parent-parent interactions. Maternal well-being affects an infant's growth and development.

Perform a complete physical examination. Certain aspects of the exam will be important to concentrate on at certain ages, such as the red reflex and hips in young infants or pubertal development in preadolescents and adolescents. Refer to .
Assess development at every visit. See chapter on developmental and intellectual delay. Refer children with developmental delay to early intervention programs.

For school-age children, ascertain school readiness: physical health, motor development, how does the child learn (temperament and curiosity), language/speech/vocabulary, general knowledge. School performance may reveal a learning disability or focusing difficulty.

A child will begin to manifest her temperament shortly after birth. Once a parent appreciates the child's temperament, he or she will better understand the child: how she responds to her environment, how she can be soothed and self-soothes. The parent will be better able to nurture, calm, and discipline the child.

Discipline needs to be age and developmental stage appropriate. The goal of discipline should be to teach with respect and patience, not to punish and belittle. Discipline should include instruction, positive reinforcement, and punishment.

The punishment needs to be immediate, consistent, and reasonable. The punishment needs to be directed at the behavior and not the child. Time-outs when used on young children have been shown to be effective.
Physical punishment has been associated with child abuse, domestic violence, poor self-esteem, future drug abuse, and depression.

Refer to , for specific immunization recommendations by age, assuming the child is up-to-date on his/her vaccines. For information on immunization schedules and catch-up, review the CDC recommended vaccination schedules.
Timely administration of immunizations prevents disease and protects children from numerous diseases.

Missed opportunities to immunize children result from physicians' misunderstanding of immunization contraindications, unwillingness to administer more than three injectable vaccines, and parental objections. One study found that fully immunizing any young child who is under-immunized and presents for a well child visit can have a significant impact on the number of fully immunized children by 2 years of age.

Immunization goals are to immunize children in a timely fashion and fully immunize when the opportunity presents itself, ideally during a well child visit. Immunizing children in the urgent care setting decreased the number of well child visits.
summarizes UK vaccination recommendations.
Screening urinalysis of asymptomatic children is not cost effective and is not recommended.
Lead screening should be considered if the child's family is living in a pre-1946 home, is non-Hispanic Black or Hispanic, or low income.

Hemoglobin or hematocrit is recommended at 12 months of age and, after that, if at risk. High risk patients include infants, toddlers, adolescents and pregnant women due to rapid growth and increased demands. Some children with iron deficiency anemia may have normal hemoglobin and hematocrit.

PPD is recommended, if at risk, starting at 12 months of age. Risk factors include foreign birth, foreign travel, ingestion of raw milk, close association with individuals with tuberculosis or latent tuberculosis infection, and exposure to individuals who have been incarcerated, living in a shelter, or with HIV.

AAP guidelines recommend that a fasting lipid panel should be considered for children with risk factors after age 2 years and no later than 10 years of age. Risk factors include family history of dyslipidemia or premature cardiovascular disease (<56 years of age for men, <66 years of age for women), unknown family history, and if the patient is overweight (BMI between the 84th and 95th percentiles) or obese (BMI >94th percentile), hypertensive (BP >95th percentile), smokes, or has diabetes mellitus. If the results are normal, repeat test every 3 to 5 years. Screening is not recommended for children less than 2 years of age. However, the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) concluded that evidence was insufficient to recommend for or against screening for dyslipidemia in children.

Vision screening starts at 3 years of age and is performed at each well child visit. 5% to 10% of pre-school children have vision problems; 4% of these children have strabismus (misalignment of eyes). Visual acuity is improved with screening. Amblyopia (loss of visual acuity due to cortical suppression) treatment is more effective if initiated prior to 3 years of age.

Hearing screening is recommended to start at 4 years of age and is done at each well child visit until 11 years of age. Screening is continued after 11 years of age if the child is at risk. Some risk factors include family history of sensorineural hearing loss, ear or craniofacial anomalies, bacterial meningitis, recurrent otitis media, ototoxic medication, trauma to nervous system, and damaging noise levels.
Sexually transmitted disease screening may be considered for sexually active patients. The USPSTF recommends against screening for cervical dysplasia in females under the age of 21 years.
Screening for adverse childhood experiences and unmet social needs improves identification and referral to services.
Anticipatory guidance addresses concerns of parents and patients and offers information in a useful manner in an effort to guide and improve one's parenting and the child's overall health.
Tailor anticipatory guidance to the child's developmental stage and parental concerns.
Anticipatory guidance often includes discussion of nutrition and safety.

Breastfeed exclusively for the first 4 to 6 months of life. Studies have shown a decrease in gastrointestinal infections and increases in verbal and performance IQs. Infants who are exclusively breastfed should be given daily oral vitamin D supplementation of 400 international units daily.
Infants who are not exclusively breastfed should be fed an iron-fortified formula.
Encourage routine mealtimes with three meals a day and appropriate snacks.
Encourage a well-balanced diet, including recommended amounts of fruits, vegetables, and milk. Eat breakfast every day.
Limit eating out, fast food, sugar-sweetened drinks, and portions. Encourage family mealtimes (usually higher quality food).
Evaluate for eating disorder.
Evaluate for fluoride supplementation to prevent dental caries.
Determine level of and encourage physical activity.
Limit screen time to none for those under 2 years of age, and 1 to 2 hours for children 2 years and older.
Repetitive safety education at well child visits improves parental safety knowledge and safety practices.
At the newborn and young infant visits, discuss sleep position, location, and crib safety.
Counsel parents to stop smoking. Secondhand smoke exposure is related to otitis media, respiratory distress, and asthma.
In infants younger than 1 year, reinforce the use of rear-facing car seats in the back seat.
With older children, discuss bicycle helmets, swimming and water safety, and outdoor supervision.

In adolescents, screen for safety/behavior issues without the parent present in the room. The HEADSS talk consists of Home, Education/Employment, Activity, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide/Depression, Safety.

feature.caption: Recommended Content of Well Child Visits from 1 Week to 6 Months of Age.

tr.td: Awake during feedings; responsive to parents' voices; fixes on face; follows to midline.
Height, weight, OFC.

Complete exam, with emphasis on skin (jaundice); eye (red reflex, clear corneas); heart (refer to chapter on Heart Murmur); hips (dysplasia; refer to chapter on Abnormal Gait in Children); muscle tone.
Newborn screen (if not done); hearing and vision, if at risk.
Support; maternal well-being; sleep position; car seat; smoke exposure; breastfeeding exclusively first 4-6 months; feed every 2-3 hrs; minimize exposures to large groups; frequent hand-washing.
Follows parents; responsive to parents' voices; smiles.
Ht, Wt, OFC; Complete exam, emphasis on: eyes (red reflex); heart (murmur); hips; degree of alertness.
Hearing, if not done.

Maternal well-being; sleep position; SIDS; tummy time; frequent hand washing; car seat. Exclusive breastfeeding until 4-6 months. Start Vitamin D supplementation for breast-fed infants prior to 2 months of age.
Looks at parents; smiles, vocalizes; improving head control; follows to midline; extremities move symmetrically.
Ht, Wt, OFC complete exam with emphasis on: eyes (red reflexes); heart (murmur); hips.
DTaP, IPV, HIB, Hep B, PCV13, Rotavirus. Consider Influenza for parents.

Exclusive breastfeeding until 4-6 months; iron-fortified formula for non-breast-fed infants; sleep position; communication: talk to infant; hold infant. Use car seat. Vitamin D supplementation for breast-fed infants.
Smiles; elicits social interaction; laughs; visual following; responds to change in environment.Pushes up on elbows; good head control; beginning to roll; reaches.
Ht, Wt, OFC Complete exam with emphasis on: eyes (red reflexes); heart (murmur); hips.
DTaP, IPV, HIB, Hep B, PCV13, Rotavirus. Consider Influenza for parents.

Support for parents; consider individual time for each child; cannot spoil child; daily routines; sleep position; tummy time. Infant's temperament: how does child respond and communicate? Exclusive breastfeeding until 4-6 months. Car seat; smoke exposure.
Squeals, turns to voice; reaches; may start to sit, bears weight on legs. Rolls over.
Ht, Wt, OFC Complete exam with emphasis on: eyes (red reflex; fixes and follows with both eyes); heart (murmur); hips; muscle tone.
DTaP, IPV, HIB (depending on type); Hep B, PCV13, Rotavirus (do not give Rotavirus vaccine after 8 months of age). Consider Influenza.

Support for parents; child's temperament. Read to infant. Routine sleep and meals. Introduce solid foods; breast milk or formula until 1 year of age. Dental health ; Home safety: crawling, water. No walker.

feature.caption: Recommended Content of Well Child Visits from 9 Months to 6 Years of Age.

tr.td: Learning cause and effect; gestures wants; shows preferences; self-feeding; drinks from cup.
Ht, Wt, OFC Complete exam with emphasis on: skull deformities; eyes: (red reflex; eye movement/alignment); teeth; heart (murmur); muscle tone/strength.
Lead (9-12 months, if at risk); dental; consider influenza; catch-up immunizations.
Parental expectations; discipline: consistency. May awaken more at night. No television; read to infant. Safe environment: drownings, burns, poisoning, electrical cords.

Stranger anxiety; "mama," "dada," 1-2 other words; vocalizes; follows simple instruction; looks at books; crawls, pulls to stand; stands alone; gets to sitting, thumb-finger grasp; bangs 2 cubes. Play is interactive.
Ht, Wt, OFC Complete exam with emphasis on: eyes (red reflex, conjugate gaze); teeth; muscle tone and strength.
MMR, DTaP, HIB, PCV13, VZ, Hep A. Consider influenza; Hgb/Hct; lead (9-12 months, if at risk); PPD, if at risk; dental evaluation.

Nutrition: whole milk. 3 meals and 2 snacks a day. Appetite varies. Routines: meals, bedtime, brushing teeth, reading. Safety: medications, cleansers, firearms. Behavior and expectations of parents. Discipline: no shouting, hitting, long explanations. Be positive role model.
Imitates activity; Indicates wants by pulling, pointing, grunting. 2-3 words (in addition to "mama" and "dada"); follows simple commands; walks well; stoops and recovers; steps backward.
Ht, Wt, OFC Complete exam with emphasis on: eyes (red reflex and conjugate gaze); teeth; muscle tone, strength, gait.
DTaP, HIB, MMR, Vz, PCV13 (one of each of these should be between 12 and 18 months of age). Hep A (2 shots given 6 months apart, can initiate series at 12 months of age). Consider influenza.

More independent; temper tantrums; set limits. Discipline: goal is to teach and protect, not punish. Praise child. No hitting, spanking, shaking. Model behavior. Stranger anxiety. Speech: 4-5 words. Routines: bed, meals, reading, brushing teeth. Car seats; smoke detectors; poisons, pesticides, laundry soaps. Water safety.

Interactions with other children: aggressive, friendly, withdrawn. Helps in house. Speech: 6 words; indicates wants: pointing/gesturing. Points to 1 body part; follows one command; Stacks 2-3 blocks; scribbles.
Ht, Wt, OFC Complete exam with emphasis on: eyes (red reflex and conjugate gaze); heart (murmur); gait; muscle tone.
DTaP, MMR, Vz, PCV13, HIB, (one of each between 12 and 24 months of age). Two Hep A (between 12-24 months of age, 6 months apart). Consider influenza.

Family time: talk, play. Routines: Meals, bed, brushing teeth, reading. Sibling conflicts. Discipline: consistency, praise/reinforce appropriate behavior. Brief time-outs; teach, don't punish. Praise child. No hitting, spanking, shaking. Model behavior. Language: sing, talk, read. Toilet training. Car seats. Poisons, insecticides, laundry soap, firearms. Water safety.
Imitates adults; parallel play; 2-3 word phrases; 50 words; follows 2 commands; stacks 5-6 blocks; throws overhand; climbs stairs one at a time; kicks ball; jumps up.
Ht, Wt, OFC, BMI; complete exam with emphasis on: eyes (red reflex; conjugate eye movement); teeth; symmetrical muscle movement/ tone; gait.
Lead and lipid panel/cholesterol, if at risk. Immunizations: catch-up. Consider influenza.

Read to child. Praise, hold, talk to child. Discipline: time-outs effective. Consistency. No hitting, spanking. Positive role model. Toilet training. Limit television time; 1-2 hr/day. Car seat, bike helmets; firearms. Water safety.
Imaginative play; interactive play; 2-3 sentences together; 75% intelligibility. Knows name. Uses cup. Towers 6-8 cubes; throws overhand; rides tricycle; walks upstairs alternating feet.
Ht, Wt, BP, BMI. Complete exam with emphasis on: eyes (fundi; conjugate gaze). Muscle tone /strength. Gait. Speech; language.
Vision. Lead, if not done before. Consider hearing, Hgb, PPD, if at risk. Immunization catch-up. Consider influenza.

Do not allow biting, hitting. Immediate negative feedback. Time-outs. No hitting, spanking. Model behavior. Read, sing, describe, explain. Play together. Limit television time 1-2 hr/day. No TV or DVD in bedroom. Car seat; firearms; swimming pools.

Identifies self: gender, age. First/last name. Fantasy play. What to do if hungry, cold. Speech intelligibility: 100%. 4 colors; draws a person: 3 parts; board games. Hops one foot, skips, alternates feet going down stairs; tower 8 blocks. Brushes teeth; dresses self.
Ht, Wt, BP, BMI; complete exam with emphasis on: fundi; conjugate gaze. muscle tone/strength. Speech and communication.
DTaP, IPV, MMR, Vz, and catch-up immunizations. Consider influenza. Vision. Hearing. Consider: HgB/Hct, lead, PPD, Lipid panel if at risk. UA: no longer routinely recommended.

School readiness. Read with child. Ask questions; allow child to tell stories. Routine: bedtime, meals. Limit television time 1-2 hr/day. Encourage physical activity: running, jumping, riding. Outside supervision. Firearms, car seat, bike helmets, water safety. Discipline: consistency, positive feedback. Praise child. Immediate negative feedback. No hitting, spanking. Positive role model.

Ability to separate from parents; interacts with other children; focuses; follows directions; draws a person: 6 parts; copies triangle. 4 colors; understands 4 prepositions; hops, skips, balances one foot 3-4 seconds; climbs stairs with alternating feet. Competitive games. Dresses self.
Ht, Wt, BP, BMI. Complete exam with emphasis on: fundi, teeth, muscle tone, strength, and gait. Speech/language.
One of each between 4-6 years: DTaP, IPV, MMR, Vz. Consider influenza. Vision, Hearing. If at risk: PPD, lead, HgB/ Hct, lipid panel. UA: no longer recommended routinely.

School readiness, performance. School: friends, fears; social interactions. Dental health. Nutrition: breakfast every day, well-balanced diet. Physical activity: team sports; limit television time 1-2 hr/day. Increasing independence and responsibility. Safety: booster seats, bike helmets, water safety, inappropriate touching. Outdoor supervision. More responsible, apologizes, less aggressive, questions others. Discipline: consistency, praise child, immediate negative feedback. No hitting, spanking. Positive role model.

feature.caption: Recommended Content of Well Child Visits from 7 to 21 Years of Age.

tr.td: Relationships: outside family, best friend, peer acceptance. More responsibilities. Uses logic. School performance: attention, academic, social, physical. Tries lying, cheating. Establishing independence and self-esteem.

Immunization catch up. Consider influenza. Vision; hearing. Consider PPD, HgB/ Hct, lipid panel if at risk. UA no longer routinely recommended.

School: performance, after-school activity. Nutrition: breakfast daily. Dental hygiene. Physical activity. Limit television time 1-2 hours/day. Safety: bike helmets, seat belts, firearms, water safety, alcohol, drugs, sexuality, violence, inappropriate touching. Know friends/homes. Discipline: encourage competence. Support/ praise child. Consequences for broken rules. No spanking, hitting. Positive role model.

Ht, Wt, BP, BMI. Complete exam with emphasis on: Sexual maturation: breasts, genitalia.

Nutrition: breakfast daily, limit fast foods and sugar-sweetened drinks. Physical activity. Limit television time 1-2 hr/day. Safety: seat belts, bike helmets, firearms, drugs, alcohol, sexuality. Encourage independence, responsible behavior. Discuss pubertal changes. Discuss body image.

Relationships: friends, family, peer pressure. Stressors. School performance. Physical activity; Limit television time 1-2 hr/day (except computer homework). Diet: 3 meals a day; after-school snacks. Self-confidence.
Ht, Wt, BP, BMI. Complete exam with emphasis on: skin, breasts, genitalia, spine.

Consider: HgB/ Hct (annually for menstruating females), lipid panel, PPD, testing for sexually transmitted infections. Cervical dysplasia screening: no longer reccommended <21 years.

Nutrition: breakfast daily, adequate calcium, well-balanced diet. Physical activity. Limit television time 1-2 hours/day. Safety: seat belts, bike helmets, drugs, alcohol, sex, HEADSS discussion. Body image.
Relationships: family, friends, peer pressure. School performance. Stressors: coping skills. Diet. Goals. Self-confidence.
Ht, Wt, BP, BMI. Complete exam with emphasis on: skin, breasts, genitalia, spine.

Immunizations: catch-up. 11 years and older need one: Tdap, Meningococcal. HPV (months 0, 2, and 6) for girls. Vision. Hearing, if at risk. Hgb annually for menstruating females. Consider: influenza vaccine, PPD, lipid panel; testing for sexually transmitted infections. Cervical dysplasia screening: no longer reccommended <21 years.
Nutrition: breakfast daily. Safety: seat belts, firearms. HEADSS discussion. Physical activity. Limit television time 1-2 hr/day. Body image.

td.strong: 18 Year to 21 Year Well Child Visit

tr.td: Relationships: family, friends. Stressors: coping skills, mental health. Self-confidence, goals. Decision-making.
Ht, Wt, BP, BMI. Complete exam with emphasis on: skin, breasts, genitalia: including pelvic exam, if 21 years old; PAP smear if sexually active for 3 years.

Immunizations: catch up. HgB/ Hct for all girls. Lipid panel. Consider: vision, hearing, PPD, if at risk. Consider testing for sexually transmitted infection. Cervical dysplasia screening: no longer reccommended <21 years.
Nutrition Safety: sexuality, alcohol, drugs, smoking, violence. Physical activity. Healthy relationships.
